newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr keeps low profile as bears re-group.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr keeps low profile as bears re-group.

text.p: The Australian dollar kept a low profile atop 75 cent support at a quiet midsession as the market took stock after last week's near one cent loss.
Traders reported bids at US$0.7505, partly from exporters and options-related, while offers from offshore sources such as Swiss and New York investment banks were waiting at US$0.7530.

Interest differentials continued to move against the dollar as the money market priced in another cut in official rates here and made it expensive to hold the A$ compared to the US$. The technical outlook had also soured following the break of major US$0.7550 support and analysts expected to see US$0.7480 soon.
By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the local currency had settled at US$0.7510/15 having spent the entire morning in a paltry four tick range.
It finished at US$0.7524/29 late here Friday, almost a cent down on the week after shockingly weak employment data fanned fears the Reserve Bank could yet ease again.

Most analysts thought the bank would wait until its next monthly board meeting on July 1 to consider the matter given there was little domestic data out of note before then and the U.S. Federal Reserve held a vital monetary policy meeting on July 1-2.

Such logic was cold comfort to a market which had been badly caught out by three of the four rate cuts this cycle and traders were resigned to being tense ahead of every RBA morning operation from now on.

The money market certainly thought it a foregone conclusion with the September 90-day bank bill contract up at 94.91 after rallying more than 1/4 point last week, to imply a rate of 5.09 percent against the present cash rate of 5.50 percent.
In contrast the three month Eurodollar contract was at 94.135 implying the market expected at least a 0.25 point hike in Fed fund rates from their current 5.50 percent level.
This was a novel experience to investors as A$ rates had traditionally traded well above their U.S. counterparts since before the currency was first floated in 1983.

That was not to say it was undeserved, analysts added, noting Australian inflation had averaged less than that in the U.S. for much of the 1990's and the country was increasingly coming to grips with its fiscal and current account problems.

This was being reflected in yield spreads between Australia and the U.S. which had turned negative out to three years while the local ten year bond was barely 50 basis points above the corresponding U.S. issue, again a level not seen since 1983.
Australian inflation was also expected to slow further this year, particularly on the consumer price index where falling mortgage rates could take it comfortably under 1.0 percent.

Such an outlook contrasted with the U.S. where a tight labour market meant the pressure on inflation was upwards and should allow Australia to sustain lower short term rates without a collapse in the currency.
But that did not mean there was no more downside left near term and analysts saw scope to reach US$0.7380 or even the 1996 trough of 73 cents should the RBA indeed cut again.
